title: Sitting posture
hook: cross-legged, on a chair or a bench: a straight back, a relaxed body

segments.voice: Yesterday, one character read four ways: Chan, Seon, Thien, Zen. Your line: four names, one practice. Did you catch the word zen used for a mood? Day one thousand two hundred seven.

Take a quick inventory, right where you are. Is the head drifting forward toward a screen? Is one shoulder higher than the other? Is the lower back curled like a question mark into the couch? Nothing wrong with any of it. That's just how bodies settle when nobody is paying attention. Zen pays attention. Before any teaching about the mind, it asks a very plain question: how are you sitting? Yesterday this path said the meditation school starts with the body. Today it starts. Today's word: zazen.
screen: `HEAD FORWARD, SHOULDERS UNEVEN.` → `HOW ARE YOU SITTING?` → `ZEN STARTS WITH THE BODY.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Zazen is Japanese for seated meditation: za, sitting, and zen, the meditation school's own word. A plain name for the school's central practice. Second, the base. The classic postures are cross-legged on a firm round cushion: full lotus, with each foot resting on the opposite thigh; half lotus, with one foot up; or the easier Burmese way, both legs folded on the floor, one in front of the other. Some people kneel instead, on a cushion or a small wooden bench. Some sit on a chair, feet flat, not leaning back. Zen teachers today offer these. The point isn't the shape of the legs. It's a base that's stable, so the body can stop holding itself up by effort. Third, the spine. On that base, the back rises straight, not stiff, more like it's being stacked than braced. Some teachers describe a thread lifting gently from the crown of the head. There's an old instruction, which this path will read in full later, from Dogen's guide to sitting: ears in line with the shoulders, nose in line with the navel. It's a check anyone can do. Fourth, the pair. Straight and relaxed. Straight alone turns into a soldier at attention, tight in the jaw and shoulders, and soon tired. Relaxed alone slumps back into the couch. Zazen asks for both at once: upright enough to stay awake, soft enough to stay there. On an ordinary Tuesday, that's not a bad description of a good way to meet a hard conversation either.
screen: `ZAZEN: SEATED MEDITATION.` · `A STABLE BASE: CUSHION, BENCH, CHAIR.` · `EARS OVER SHOULDERS, NOSE OVER NAVEL.` · `STRAIGHT AND RELAXED, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `UPRIGHT ENOUGH TO STAY AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: find your posture. Whatever you're sitting on, come to the front of it, so the spine holds itself. Let the base settle: cushion, bench, chair, the floor. Rock gently side to side, then forward and back, and let each sway get smaller until you stop in the middle. Ears over shoulders. Nose over navel. Now check for straining. Let the shoulders drop. Let the belly soften. Straight, and relaxed. Then simply sit there, in that shape. The bell holds the time.
Zazen. Japanese for seated meditation, the central practice of Zen: a stable base, a straight back, a relaxed body. Today's word.
Your line: straight and relaxed. Today, each time you sit down, at a desk, in a car, at a table, find the middle again: ears over shoulders, shoulders down. Day one thousand two hundred seven.

howItsDone: In Zen centers and monasteries, people sit zazen facing a wall or the room, on round cushions over flat mats, on kneeling benches or on chairs, and beginners are usually shown how to find their posture before anything else.

myth: zazen only counts in full lotus
cushion, bench and chair are all offered; the point is a stable base.

straight and relaxed: stacked, not braced.
za, sitting, and zen, the school's word for meditation.

fork.setup: you want to try zazen, but your knees won't let you cross your legs. what do you do?
options: skip zazen; it isn't for you
sit on a chair or a bench, back upright
fork.reveal: a chair or a kneeling bench is a real zazen posture. the point is a stable base, a straight back and a relaxed body.

original.note: Japanese: za, sitting, and zen, meditation; seated meditation.

trapdoor: what you thought: zazen means sitting cross-legged and very still.
what it means: seated meditation on any stable base, with a back that is straight and a body that is relaxed.
what a scholar hears: Dogen's guide gives a plain check for the spine: ears in line with the shoulders, nose in line with the navel.

sources.ref: Dogen, Fukanzazengi (ears in line with the shoulders, nose in line with the navel)

notes: No quotations. Day 1240 covers Dogen's Fukanzazengi in full; this day only borrows the ears/shoulders, nose/navel check and says so.
'Zen teachers offer all of these' (cushion, bench, chair) and 'many people kneel / sit on a chair' are general descriptions of practice; soften if needed.
Gloss of zazen as za (sitting) + zen (meditation): a reading of the characters, not a derivation claim; confirm 坐禅 form.
The thread from the crown is attributed to 'some teachers'.
Editor pass: cut the superlative 'the plainest name possible'; softened 'Zen teachers offer all of these' to 'Zen teachers today offer these'.
